10.title: How results are calculated
10.content: What InverseHub compares on each compliance path, in plain words. The calculation on your project page shows the same steps with your numbers. On this page . | Energy cost first | Performance cost index (ASHRAE 90.1-2016 and later) | Earlier ASHRAE 90.1 editions (2007 to 2013) | Energy Cost Budget Method | Total Building Performance (IECC) | IgCC | LEED v4 with the 2024 energy update . | Energy cost or source energy | GHG emissions | . | Unmet load hours | Units | .

11.title: Energy cost first
11.content: Every path starts from the annual energy cost of each design, from the utility rates in the reports. On-site renewable energy and exceptional calculations you entered in SimReader are subtracted from the proposed design. New off-site renewable energy is subtracted only from the proposed design’s GHG emissions, for LEED v4 with the 2024 energy update.

12.title: Performance cost index (ASHRAE 90.1-2016 and later)
12.content: The proposed design complies when its performance cost index is at or below the target: . | PCI = proposed building performance ÷ baseline building performance, where both are annual energy costs. | PCIt = (baseline unregulated energy cost + BPF × baseline regulated energy cost − PRE) ÷ baseline building performance. | . Where: . | BPF is the code’s building performance factor for the building type and climate zone. With several building area types, InverseHub uses the area-weighted average. | PRE is the energy cost of the on-site renewable energy the code requires (90.1-2022 and the codes based on it). It’s zero otherwise. | On-site renewables count toward the PCI up to 5% of the baseline building performance; with a PRE, only renewables beyond the required system count. | . Energy index. With the energy method, the same formulas use site energy instead of cost. Codes with their own energy rules use their own BPF tables and conversion factors: source energy for NYC 2020, site energy for NYC 2025 and New York State 2025. ASHRAE 90.1-2022 and Oregon 2025 offer site energy, source energy or carbon. If you enter local conversion factors for electricity and gas, InverseHub recalculates the BPF from them with the code’s coefficients.

13.title: Earlier ASHRAE 90.1 editions (2007 to 2013)
13.content: The Performance Rating Method compares the proposed design’s energy cost with the baseline building’s. It passes when the proposed cost is lower. With the energy method, it compares site energy.

14.title: Energy Cost Budget Method
14.content: The design energy cost (DEC) of the proposed design must be at or below the energy cost budget (ECB), the budget building’s annual energy cost. | From 90.1-2016 on, on-site renewables are credited up to 5% of the budget. | In 90.1-2022, the budget is reduced by the required energy credits: ECB × (1 − credits ÷ 1000 × the additions and alterations factor). The required on-site solar’s cost (PRE) comes off the budget, and only renewables beyond it are credited. | .

15.title: Total Building Performance (IECC)
15.content: The proposed design’s annual energy cost must be at most a share of the standard reference design’s: . | 100% for IECC 2006 and 2009; 85% for IECC 2012 to 2021; 80% for Chicago 2022; 85% for New York State 2020. | For IECC 2018 and 2021, and Chicago 2022, on-site renewables count up to 5% of the standard reference design’s energy cost. For the other editions, they’re subtracted from the proposed cost. | .

16.title: IgCC
16.content: . | IgCC 2012 and 2015: the zero energy performance index (zEPI) compares source energy use intensities: zEPI = 57 (2012) or 52 (2015) × proposed EUI ÷ standard reference EUI. It must be at most 51 (2012) or 50 (2015). The proposed design’s CO₂e emissions are checked too. On-site renewable energy is subtracted from the proposed design’s energy and emissions. | IgCC 2021: the cost PCI and the source-energy zEPI against their targets, which the building’s renewable fraction lowers. Also checked: CO₂e emissions, and the PCI without renewables against the ASHRAE 90.1-2019 target. | Source energy and CO₂e factors come from the code. Electricity uses the factors of your project’s EPA eGRID subregion. | .

17.title: LEED v4 with the 2024 energy update
17.content: The Optimize Energy Performance points add up two metrics, each with its own thresholds for your rating system. Energy cost or source energy . InverseHub works out both savings and uses the higher one: . | Energy cost savings = 1 − proposed annual energy cost ÷ baseline annual energy cost, after on-site renewable energy and exceptional calculations (see Energy cost first). | Source energy savings = 1 − proposed source energy ÷ baseline source energy. Each design’s source energy is each fuel’s annual site energy times its source-to-site ratio, added up. On-site renewable energy counts as zero source energy: it reduces the proposed design’s purchased electricity, up to all of it. Exceptional calculation savings are subtracted at their fuel’s ratio. | . The LEED Minimum Energy Performance Calculator accepts two sets of source-to-site ratios. InverseHub works out source energy savings with both and keeps the set that gives the higher savings, so it never gives fewer points. A line under the points in the conclusion names the set used and the other set’s result. | Energy type | ASHRAE 90.1-2022 | ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager | Canada | . | Electricity | 2.64 | 2.80 | 1.83 | . | Natural gas | 1.09 | 1.05 | 1.06 | . | Propane | 1.15 | 1.01 | 1.00 | . | Fuel oil and diesel | 1.19 | 1.01 | 1.00 | . | District heating | 1.20 | 1.20 | 1.33 | . | District cooling | 0.91 | 0.91 | 0.57 | . | Other fuels | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | . | ASHRAE 90.1-2022 gives no ratios for district energy, so both US sets use Portfolio Manager’s. | Canadian projects use Portfolio Manager’s ratios for Canada, the only set there. | Projects in other countries are worked out with both US sets, as above. | . GHG emissions . GHG emissions reduction = 1 − proposed emissions ÷ baseline emissions. Each design’s emissions are each fuel’s annual site energy times its emission factor, added up. | Electricity uses the CO₂e factor of the project’s EPA eGRID 2022 subregion, chosen under General Information, as in the LEED Minimum Energy Performance Calculator. Without a subregion, the US average applies; outside the US and Canada, the country’s national average. | Canada: choose the province or territory in the same field. Electricity uses the calculator’s factor for it, below, and natural gas 116.4 lb CO₂e per MMBtu. The conclusion asks for the province or territory first. | Other fuels, in lb CO₂e per MMBtu: natural gas 117.8, propane 139.1, fuel oil and diesel 163.6, gasoline 155.3, coal 209.4, district heating 147.3, district cooling 116.9. Fuel oil and diesel entered in gallons count 137.381 kBtu per gallon at the same factor, about 22.5 lb per gallon. | Subtracted from the proposed design: on-site renewable energy and exceptional calculation savings at their fuel’s factor, and new off-site renewable energy at its grid region’s factor. Off-site renewable energy counts for this metric only. | . Canada’s electricity factors, in lb CO₂e per MMBtu: . | Province or territory | Factor | Province or territory | Factor | . | Alberta | 403.0 | Nunavut | 520.0 | . | British Columbia | 8.5 | Ontario | 18.2 | . | Manitoba | 0.8 | Prince Edward Island | 156.0 | . | New Brunswick | 156.0 | Quebec | 1.2 | . | Newfoundland and Labrador | 16.3 | Saskatchewan | 403.0 | . | Nova Scotia | 117.0 | Yukon | 71.5 | . | Northwest Territories | 448.5 |   |   | .

27.title: Show compliance
27.content: Add the calculations your compliance path needs, then let InverseHub write the conclusion. Both follow the energy code and rating system in Energy Model Information. On this page . | The two steps, on every path | Performance Rating Method (ASHRAE 90.1 Appendix G) . | 90.1-2016 and later, and the codes built on them | 90.1-2007, 2010 and 2013 | . | Energy Cost Budget Method (ASHRAE 90.1) | Total Building Performance (IECC) | IgCC Performance Option | LEED and other programs | Massachusetts | Living Building Challenge, Zero Carbon and Zero Energy | Unmet load hours | .

28.title: The two steps, on every path
28.content: . | Calculations: select + on the calculations card. Its name follows the path: Performance Calculations, Energy Cost Budget Calculations, Total Building Performance Calculations or zEPI Calculations. | Conclusion: select + on Conclusion. InverseHub checks the results against the code and writes a short pass or fail statement: the result with its numbers, then the requirement. For example: “Pass. The Performance Cost Index (PCI) is 0.42, 20.7% below the target (PCIt) of 0.53. It must be at most the PCIt.” When the design passes, it adds the compliance statement, for example: “The building performance meets the minimum performance required by the Performance Rating Method of ASHRAE Standard 90.1-2019.” | . To redo either, delete it with its trash icon and add it again; the saved text doesn’t update by itself. Change the inputs with the edit icon on the calculation. The review page’s summary shows the conclusion’s key figures, such as LEED points, the PCI against the PCIt or the 179D deduction. They’re saved when you add the conclusion, and editing its text keeps them. For a conclusion added before October 23, 2026, the summary works them out from the results. A conclusion that uses conversion factors or ratios ends with a small gray line listing the ones it used, for the fuels in your results. These include GHG emission factors, source-to-site ratios and a code’s own source energy or carbon factors. A conclusion added before October 25, 2026 shows the line once you add it again or refresh it. When you change an input the conclusion uses, InverseHub checks whether its figures move. Saving a new eGRID subregion, other General Information such as the country or areas, or the zEPI calculations then shows Conclusion out of date with each figure that changes. The Conclusion card also shows a reminder until the conclusion is updated. Refresh deletes the conclusion and adds it again from the current inputs. Edits you made to its text are lost; reviewers’ comments are kept.

29.title: Performance Rating Method (ASHRAE 90.1 Appendix G)
29.content: 90.1-2016 and later, and the codes built on them . Compliance is a performance cost index (PCI) at or below its target (PCIt). The target comes from the code’s building performance factors (BPFs). | On Performance Calculations, select +. | Choose the Performance Index Calculation Method: . | Performance Cost Index Method: energy cost, as the standard requires. | Performance Energy Index Method: site energy. Codes with their own energy rules name their method here instead. For example, NYC 2020 uses source energy, NYC 2025 site energy, and ASHRAE 90.1-2022 and Oregon 2025 let you pick site energy, source energy or carbon, optionally with local conversion factors. | . | Choose the BPF Calculation: the code’s defaults for your climate zone, or a Custom BPF. | Enter the floor area of each Building Area Type. The effective BPF is the area-weighted average. BPFs cover conditioned floor area only. | For 90.1-2022 and the codes based on it, enter the annual output of any on-site solar the code requires. Its value comes off the target, and only renewables beyond it count toward the 5% renewables credit. | Select Add Calculations. | . The card then shows the result with each step of the calculation. If you pick a method the code doesn’t allow, a red note says so in the dialog, the calculation and the conclusion. The conclusion then leaves out the compliance sentence: the result is for reference only. 90.1-2007, 2010 and 2013 . There are no BPFs. The conclusion compares the proposed design’s energy cost with the baseline’s: it passes when the proposed cost is lower. With the energy method, it compares site energy instead.

30.title: Energy Cost Budget Method (ASHRAE 90.1)
30.content: Compliance is the design energy cost (the proposed design’s) at or below the energy cost budget (the budget building’s). | On Energy Cost Budget Calculations, select +. For 90.1-2022 and the codes based on it, enter the energy credits required, the additions and alterations factor and the annual output of the required on-site solar. Earlier editions need no inputs here. | Add the conclusion. | . On-site renewables are subtracted from the design energy cost. From 90.1-2016 on, they’re credited up to 5% of the budget. Requirements the edition sets beyond the cost comparison are listed in the calculation as “also required, not checked here”.

33.title: LEED and other programs
33.content: For LEED rating systems, the conclusion gives the points for the Optimize Energy Performance credit under the LEED version you chose. The Massachusetts paths (below) and 179D have their own conclusions too. For NGBS with IECC 2018, the 2020 NGBS baseline, the conclusion gives the Energy Efficiency points and level. The points are 30 plus 2 for each percent of energy cost savings over the IECC standard reference design, rounded down: Bronze at 30 points (meets the IECC), Silver at 45 (7.5%), Gold at 60 (15%) and Emerald at 70 (20%). With other IECC editions, the conclusion compares the energy cost with the baseline. On the 2024 Update, the points add up two metrics: the higher of energy cost savings and source energy savings, and the GHG emissions reduction. InverseHub works out source energy with both sets of source-to-site ratios the LEED calculator accepts, ASHRAE 90.1-2022’s and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager’s, and uses the set with the higher savings. The line under the points names it, with the other set’s result, and lists the ratios and GHG factors used. Canadian projects use Portfolio Manager’s ratios for Canada and their province’s or territory’s GHG factors, chosen under General Information. The ratios, emission factors and what’s subtracted are in How results are calculated. LEED v4.1 and the LEED v4 pilot credit (ACP 110) also score GHG emissions. Their electricity uses the same factors: the eGRID subregion, or a Canadian project’s province or territory, chosen under General Information. For LEED ID+C on the 2024 Update, adding the conclusion first asks which baseline envelope you modeled: New construction or Existing conditions before renovation. The conclusion and the review page’s summary then give the points for that envelope only. To switch, delete the conclusion and add it again. On the 2024 Update, new off-site renewable energy entered in SimReader counts toward the GHG emissions reduction only, not toward energy cost or source energy. Each system’s emissions offset uses its grid region’s eGRID factor. The conclusion says how much of the reduction it gives. The project page shows each system’s offset and, for your Renewable Energy credit, its share of the proposed design’s site energy and GHG emissions before renewables. InverseHub doesn’t calculate the Renewable Energy credit’s points.

48.title: What are the necessary setups for reading EnergyPlus outputs?
48.content: SimReader reads the LEED Summary, Building Energy Performance and Tariff Report tables in eplustbl.html. If they’re missing, add the output tables to your IDF file and run the simulation again. The objects to copy are in EnergyPlus and OpenStudio.

49.title: Which simulation programs work with InverseHub?
49.content: eQUEST (DOE-2) and EnergyPlus, including the programs that run EnergyPlus, such as OpenStudio and DesignBuilder. See Prepare your model output.

50.title: Where can I locate the energy model results?
50.content: eQUEST writes .SIM files next to the project’s .pd2 and .inp files. EnergyPlus writes eplustbl.html in the run’s output folder. See Where to find the report files.

51.title: Why doesn’t SimReader list my project?
51.content: SimReader lists only pinned projects. Pin the project in InverseHub, then select Refresh next to Project Name in SimReader.

52.title: Can I average several baseline runs?
52.content: Yes. Add all the baseline files (for example the four orientations) to Baseline(s), and SimReader averages them. The first file supplies the utility rates and unmet load hours.

53.title: Why can’t I choose the Performance Rating Method for an IECC project?
53.content: Each energy code lists only its own compliance paths, and the IECC’s is Total Building Performance. If your project uses the ASHRAE 90.1 alternative the IECC allows, choose that 90.1 edition as the Energy Code Used.

54.title: Can I change the baseline values after Fill Baseline?
54.content: Yes. Fill Baseline only writes text into the Baseline column. Edit any row afterwards, and replace placeholders such as “x.xx EER” with your project’s values.

55.title: Do reviewers need an InverseHub account?
55.content: No. Anyone with the link can view the report and comment on it after confirming their email with a code. People you invite comment straight from the invitation email. Only clients who follow all their projects need an account.

56.title: How do I bring back a phase I removed?
56.content: Add it again with Add a Phase, or upload it again from SimReader. Its earlier results come back.

57.title: What are SimReader default units?
57.content: kWh for electricity, therm for natural gas, gallons for fuel oil, MBtu for district energy and kBtu for the other fuels. The full table is in SimReader units.

58.title: What happens if I don’t renew my subscription?
58.content: You keep all your projects and can still open, edit and share them. Your account moves to the free Starter plan, which allows 3 new projects a month. See Account and subscription.

67.title: Glossary
67.content: Terms you’ll meet in InverseHub and SimReader. Analysis type Standard Baseline, Custom Baseline or Parametric Analysis: what a project compares. Set when you create the project; SimReader takes it from the project. Appendix G The Performance Rating Method of ASHRAE 90.1: the proposed design against a baseline building the standard defines. Appendix I An informative appendix of ASHRAE 90.1-2022 with performance targets in site energy, source energy or carbon instead of energy cost. Baseline building, budget building, standard reference design The comparison building of each path: the baseline building for the Performance Rating Method, the budget building for the Energy Cost Budget Method, the standard reference design for IECC Total Building Performance. BPF (building performance factor) The code’s factor, by building type and climate zone, that sets how much better than the baseline a design must perform (Performance Rating Method, 90.1-2016 and later). Comment code The 4-digit code emailed to someone who comments on a shared report, to confirm their email. It works for 15 minutes. InverseHub no longer uses PINs. DEC and ECB Design energy cost (the proposed design’s) and energy cost budget (the budget building’s), compared by the Energy Cost Budget Method. ECM Energy conservation measure, compared with the base design in a Parametric Analysis project. eGRID subregion The EPA region of the electricity grid that serves the project. It sets the source energy and carbon factors of electricity for the IgCC and some other codes. For LEED in Canada, the same field holds the province or territory. Exceptional calculation Savings the simulation program can’t model, calculated separately and subtracted from the proposed design. Modeling phase A stage of the project (Schematic Design, Design Development, Construction Documents, Preliminary Review, Final Review, Approved, Post-Construction). Each keeps its own results and inputs. PCI and PCIt Performance cost index (the proposed design’s energy cost over the baseline building’s) and its target. A design complies when its PCI is at or below the PCIt. PRE The energy cost of the on-site renewable energy a code requires (ASHRAE 90.1-2022 and the codes based on it). It comes off the target or the budget. Process load Energy use the code doesn’t regulate (for example kitchen or computer equipment). Mark process end uses in SimReader with Process. Renewable fraction The share of a building’s energy the IgCC 2021 expects from renewables. It lowers the IgCC 2021 targets. Unmet load hours Hours when a design’s HVAC doesn’t keep the zones at their set points. A total over 300 hours is flagged in red. zEPI Zero energy performance index of the IgCC: the proposed design’s source energy use intensity on a scale where 100 is a typical building and 0 is net zero.

82.title: DesignBuilder
82.content: DesignBuilder runs EnergyPlus, so the EnergyPlus tables above apply. To get the report file, open Simulation > Summary and select Export in the Help panel.

83.title: Where to find the report files
83.content: | Software | File | Where | . | eQUEST | .SIM (one per run) | The folder of the .pd2 and .inp files, usually Documents\eQUEST 3-65 Projects\{project} | . | EnergyPlus | eplustbl.html | The folder of the .idf file, or the output folder you chose for the run | . | OpenStudio | eplustbl.html or eplustbl.htm | {folder of the .osm}\{model name}\reports\ or \run\ | . | DesignBuilder | eplustbl.htm | Exported from Simulation > Summary (see above) | .

84.title: Units SimReader uses
84.content: SimReader converts every report to the same units, whatever the report uses (joules, GJ, MMBtu and so on). See SimReader units. Next: Read and upload results with SimReader .

85.title: Projects and phases
85.content: A project holds one building’s results, phase by phase, from Schematic Design to Post-Construction. On this page . | Choose the analysis type . | Change the analysis type | . | Your plan’s project limit | Your Home tab | Your Projects tab | Pin the projects you’re working on | Modeling phases | Project details | Clients and contacts | Delete a project | .

86.title: Choose the analysis type
86.content: You choose it in New Project. SimReader takes it from the project when you choose the project there. | Analysis type | Use it for | First tab of the project | . | Standard Baseline: Energy Code Baseline vs. Proposed Design | Code compliance and LEED, against the baseline an energy code defines | Summary Statement | . | Custom Baseline: User-Defined Baseline vs. Proposed Design | Two designs compared: a baseline you define, such as an existing building or an earlier design, and the proposed design | Summary Statement | . | Parametric Analysis: Base Design vs. ECMs, or a Base Design alone | Energy conservation measures compared with a base design, or one design reported on its own | Base Design | . One design only? For a report of one design, such as for SEDI, choose Parametric Analysis and upload just the base design, with no ECMs. The review page and the PDF then show that design alone, with no savings. A baseline project always compares two different designs. Change the analysis type . On the Projects tab, open the project’s menu (⋮), select Change Analysis Type, choose the type and select Save. If results are already uploaded, upload each phase’s results again from SimReader with the new type, then add the conclusion again. The existing results were read for the old type.

87.title: Your plan’s project limit
87.content: Each plan allows a number of new projects a month (3 on the free Starter plan). The Plan box on your Home tab, and New Project on the Projects tab, show how many you have left. See Subscription plans.

88.title: Your Home tab
88.content: Your Home tab shows what needs you and where your pinned projects stand. | Needs your reply lists the projects with open comments from reviewers and clients: how many, from whom and when. Select Open comments to go straight to the project’s Comments tab. When nothing is waiting, it isn’t shown. | Project Status counts your pinned projects by status. Click a number to show only those projects, or All to show them all again. | Each pinned project’s card shows its status, rating system and client. The boxes show the conclusion’s main figure, such as LEED points or the PCI with Pass or Fail, then Cost savings and open Comments. Before a conclusion is added, the first box says Not yet. A parametric project shows its number of ECMs and when its results were uploaded instead. Point to a box to see its details. The current phase and the results date are under the boxes. The projects with the latest activity come first. Click a card’s status to change it. | Plan shows your plan and how many new projects you’ve used this month (or billing period). | .

89.title: Your Projects tab
89.content: The Projects tab lists all your projects, grouped by client. Projects without a client are under No client. | Type in Search projects to find a project by its name, client or description. Choose a status, or tick Pinned only, to narrow the list. | Archived projects are hidden. Tick Show archived, or choose Archived as the status, to list them. They show in gray, with no pin. | Each row shows the project’s status and current phase, when its results were uploaded, and its open comments. Design alternatives are listed under their project. | A parametric project is tagged Parametric, or Base design only when its current phase’s results have no ECMs. Your client sees Base Design Only too. | Click a project’s status to change it. | The pin shows whether the project is pinned: select it to pin or unpin the project. | The menu (⋮) has Assign Client, Edit Description, Change Analysis Type and Delete. | New Project shows how many new projects you have left. | .

90.title: Pin the projects you’re working on
90.content: Pinned projects are listed on your Home tab, and they’re the only ones SimReader lists under Project Name. | On the Projects tab, select the pin next to the project’s name. It’s teal when the project is pinned. | On the project page, select Pinned to unpin it, or Pin to Home to pin it. | .

91.title: Modeling phases
91.content: Each phase keeps its own results, model inputs, calculations and conclusion. Choose the phase at the top of the project page under Modeling Phase. The phases are: . | Schematic Design: Preliminary Model, Final Model | Design Development: Preliminary Model, Final Model | Construction Documents: Preliminary Model, Final Model | Preliminary Review Model and Final Review Model: the models for each round of review, such as LEED’s preliminary and final reviews or a plan review and its resubmission | Approved Model | Post-Construction Model | . SimReader uploads results to the phase you choose in its Modeling Phase list, and offers to create the phase if it doesn’t exist yet. Use the Phase menu next to the phase list to: . | Add a Phase: optionally Copy from the current phase, which copies its model inputs, calculations and conclusion, but not its results or comments. | Move This Phase: move this phase’s content to a phase that’s still empty. | Remove This Phase: a project needs at least two phases. To bring a removed phase back, add it again with Add a Phase, or upload it again from SimReader. | .

92.title: Project details
92.content: . | General Information (project name, address, building type and floor areas): select Edit on its card. The building type and areas are used by Fill Baseline and the performance calculations. | Status: click the project’s status on the Projects tab or on its Home card, choose the new one and select Save. The status shows on your Home tab and to your client. | Archived: only you can archive a project. Archiving unpins it, so it leaves your Home and SimReader, and hides it from your client: it leaves their lists and its report no longer opens for them. Choose another status to bring it back; pin it again if you want it on your Home. | Description: on the Projects tab, open the project’s menu (⋮) and select Edit Description. | Copy Inputs from Another Project: in Energy Model Inputs, open the menu (⋮). It copies the input rows from one of your other projects. | Design alternatives: select + after the tabs to attach another of your projects as an alternative. It appears as its own tab. | .

93.title: Clients and contacts
93.content: . | Clients tab: add the companies you work for. Assign a client to a project with Assign Client in the project’s menu (⋮) on the Projects tab. | Contacts tab: the people you work with. A contact linked to a client can get an invitation (Send Invitations) to create an InverseHub account and follow that client’s projects. See Clients. | .

94.title: Delete a project
94.content: On the Projects tab, open the project’s menu (⋮) and select Delete. This deletes all its phases and results. Next: Read and upload results with SimReader .

95.title: Review a shared project
95.content: Someone shared an InverseHub report with you. You can read it and comment on it without an account: to comment, you confirm your email once with a code. On this page . | Read the report | Comment on the report | Send your comments to the modeler | Replies | .

96.title: Read the report
96.content: Open the link from the modeler’s email or message. The page shows one modeling phase of the project, starting with a summary. | The summary shows where the project stands: its status and the steps still to come, when the results were uploaded, and the modeler and their email. | Its tiles show the results that matter for the project’s purpose, followed by the energy code: . | LEED: the points for the Optimize Energy Performance credit and the metrics they come from, such as energy cost savings and the GHG reduction; | a compliance path: how far the design is below or above its target, such as the PCI against the PCIt, with Pass or Fail; | 179D: the estimated deduction; | otherwise: the energy cost savings, the annual cost savings and the site energy savings. | . | These figures come from the modeler’s conclusion. If the results were uploaded again after it, a note says so. For a conclusion added before October 23, 2026, they’re worked out from the results the same way. The summary ends with the start of the conclusion. Select Read the full conclusion to jump to all of it. | The section links under the summary take you to each part of the report: General, Model Inputs, Utility Rates, End Use, Monthly, Performance, Calculations, Conclusion and others, depending on the project. A number on a link counts the open comments in that section. Top at the bottom right brings you back up. | Model input rows with nothing entered are left out, so you only read what the modeler filled in. | Download PDF saves the report as a file. | Copy Link copies the page’s link, to pass it on to a colleague. | The Comments tab lists every comment on this phase, with the modeler’s replies. | .

97.title: Comment on the report
97.content: . | Point to the value you want to comment on and click the comment icon that appears next to it. On a phone, tap the value. Or select Add Comments. | The first time, enter your name and email, then select Send Code. Enter the 4-digit code we email you, then select Confirm. The code works for 15 minutes. | Type your comment and save it. | . Your browser then remembers you for 30 days. The top of the report shows Commenting as your name; select Not you? to switch, for example on a shared computer. For a comment on the whole report rather than one value, open the Comments tab, type it in the box at the top, and select Add Comment. You can edit or delete your own comments: select one in the table, or select Edit next to it on the Comments tab, and choose Edit Your Comment. Other people’s comments are read-only for you. Invited by the modeler? The invitation email’s Access Report button lets you comment without a code. On another device, confirm the email the invitation came to with a code. The modeler chooses who can comment through the link. If the report shows View only, only the client can comment: you can read it and download the PDF. If only the client and invited reviewers can comment, use the email your invitation came to.

98.title: Send your comments to the modeler
98.content: When you’ve finished commenting, tell the modeler in one go: . | Open the Comments tab. | Select Send my comments to the modeler. | . The modeler gets one email listing your open comments on this phase, with a link to the project. The button shows when you have open comments on the phase. If you add more later, send again: each email lists all your comments that are still open. On the Comments tab you can also: . | choose All, Open or Resolved to filter the list; | select Show in the table to jump to the value a comment is on, highlighted for a moment. | .

99.title: Replies
99.content: When the modeler replies to your comment or resolves it, you get an email with their reply and a link back to the report. The reply also appears under your comment and on the Comments tab. A resolved comment means the modeler considers it addressed.

101.title: Set up InverseHub and SimReader
101.content: You need an InverseHub account to create projects, and SimReader to upload results from your computer. On this page . | 1. Create your InverseHub account | 2. Install SimReader | 3. Sign in to SimReader | Before your first upload | .

102.title: 1. Create your InverseHub account
102.content: . | Go to inversehub.com and select Sign up. | Enter your email and a password. The password needs at least 6 characters, with an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a digit and a symbol. | Open the confirmation email and select the link. You can sign in once your email is confirmed. | . Every account starts on the free Starter plan, with 3 new projects a month. See Subscription plans for more.

103.title: 2. Install SimReader
103.content: SimReader is a free Windows app that reads your simulation reports and uploads them to InverseHub. | Install it from the Microsoft Store. | .

104.title: 3. Sign in to SimReader
104.content: . | Open SimReader and select Settings at the bottom of the side menu. | Under User, select Sign in. | Enter your InverseHub email and password, then select Sign in. Tick Remember me to stay signed in on this computer. | . When you’re signed in, the User section shows your email and a Sign out button.

105.title: Before your first upload
105.content: . | Utility rates in the model. InverseHub compares the designs by energy cost, so each model needs its utility rates. | The right reports. eQUEST writes what SimReader needs by default. EnergyPlus and OpenStudio need a few extra output tables. See Prepare your model output. | . Next: Your first project .

107.title: Share and handle comments
107.content: Share a phase as a link, collect comments, answer them, and send a PDF. On this page . | Three ways to share | Choose who can comment | Invite people to comment | Answer comments | Download a PDF | Choose what reviewers see | .

108.title: Three ways to share
108.content: | You want them to | Do this | They need | . | View and comment | Copy Link at the top of the project page, then send the link | Nothing. Anyone with the link can view it, and comments after confirming their email with a code. They can pass the link on. | . | Comment, invited by you | Email them an invitation from the Project Team tab | The invitation’s Access Report button: they comment without a code. No account. | . | Follow all their projects | Invite your client’s contacts from the Contacts tab | An InverseHub client account. See Clients. | . The link always shows the phase currently selected under Modeling Phase on your project page. If you switch to another phase later, people with the link see that one.

109.title: Choose who can comment
109.content: Your client, signed in, can always comment on their projects, with no extra step. For everyone else, the Copy Link dialog asks Who can comment through the link. Your choice is saved as soon as you pick it, and applies to the project’s link wherever it was sent: . | Anyone with the link: they confirm their email with a code. New projects start here. | My client and invited reviewers: the people on the Project Team tab, from their invitation or with a code sent to the email they were invited with. | My client only: everyone else sees View only and can’t add comments. Comments already made stay on the Comments tab. | .

110.title: Invite people to comment
110.content: . | On the project page, open the Project Team tab. | Select Add from Contacts and choose the people. Add new people on the Contacts tab of your Home page first. | Select their cards (click a card to select it), then Email Invitation. | . Each person gets an email whose Access Report button lets them comment right away, for 90 days. On another device, or later, they confirm the email they were invited with by a code, so there’s no PIN to keep. Their card then shows Invited. With Anyone with the link, an invitation is optional.

111.title: Answer comments
111.content: Reviewers comment on a table cell. A comment icon then appears in that cell, and the Comments tab lists every comment of the phase. When a reviewer or client selects Send my comments to the modeler, you get one email listing their open comments, with a link to the project. Projects with open comments are also listed under Needs your reply on your Home tab. | Select the comment to open it. | Type your reply and select Resolve to close it, or keep it open. | Reopen brings back a resolved comment, with your reply kept. | . A general comment, on the whole report rather than one value, appears first on the Comments tab. Select Reply or resolve under it to answer it the same way. The person who wrote the comment gets an email with your reply when you save a new or changed reply, and when you resolve the comment. Each comment shows the name and email its author confirmed.

112.title: Download a PDF
112.content: Select Download PDF at the top of the project page. The file is named “Project – Phase – date”. It shows the same sections as the review page, including the charts and cards you’ve switched on.

113.title: Choose what reviewers see
113.content: . | Charts: each monthly chart has a Shown / Hidden switch. | Unmet Load Hours: hidden until you switch it on. | Phase: reviewers see the phase selected on your project page. Select the phase to share before you send the link. | . Next: What reviewers see .

114.title: SimReader units
114.content: SimReader converts every report into these units, whatever the report itself uses (joules, GJ, MMBtu and so on), so baseline and proposed results always line up. | Energy type | Consumption | Peak demand | . | Electricity | kWh | kW | . | Natural gas | therm | therm/h | . | Gasoline | therm | therm/h | . | Fuel oil | gal | gal/min | . | Propane | kBtu | kBtu/h | . | Diesel | kBtu | kBtu/h | . | Coal | kBtu | kBtu/h | . | Other fuel | kBtu | kBtu/h | . | District cooling | MBtu | MBtu/h | . | District heating | MBtu | MBtu/h | . Totals across energy types (for example “Baseline in kBtu” in Total Energy Performance) are in kBtu. A gallon converts by its fuel: 137.381 kBtu for fuel oil and diesel, 91.452 kBtu for propane and 120.214 kBtu for gasoline. Other fuels in gallons use the fuel oil value.

115.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
115.title: Read and upload results with SimReader
115.content: SimReader reads your baseline and proposed reports, shows the results for you to check, then uploads them to a phase of your InverseHub project. On this page . | The Project page . | Which files go where | . | The Results page | Upload to InverseHub | Save your SimReader project | After the upload: split an end use | .

116.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
116.title: The Project page
116.content: . | Project Name: your pinned InverseHub projects. Select Refresh to reload the list after you pin a project. | Modeling Phase and Client Name: filled in from InverseHub. Reload from InverseHub fetches them again. If you change the client here, the upload changes it for every phase of the project. | Analysis Type: set by the project you choose under Project Name, and locked. If SimReader had another type selected, it switches and tells you, so check that your files are in the right lists. To change a project’s type, see Change the analysis type. With no project chosen, for example when you only read results, you can pick any type. | Files: drag .SIM, .htm or .html files onto the tiles, or select a tile to browse. | . Which files go where . | Analysis type | Left tile | Right tile | . | Standard or Custom Baseline | Baseline(s): one or more baseline runs. Several runs (such as the four orientations) are averaged. | Proposed: one file. If you add several, they’re averaged too. | . | Parametric Analysis | Base Design: one file. | ECM(s): one file per measure, numbered in list order. Leave it empty to report the base design alone. | . The order matters. The first file in each list supplies the utility rates, the DOE-2 or EnergyPlus version and the unmet load hours. Use the up and down arrows, or drag a file within its list, to reorder. Remove takes the selected files off the list. Select Next: Results when the files are in place.

117.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
117.title: The Results page
117.content: . SimReader reads the files as you arrive, and again whenever the file list changes. Reload reads them again, for example after you rerun a simulation. ‹ Edit files goes back to the Project page. Check each section before uploading: . | Utility Rates: the rate of each meter in each design. Untick Include? to leave a meter out. If the baseline and proposed rate names differ, SimReader warns you after reading. | On-Site Renewable Energy Production and Exceptional Calculation: select + Add to enter them. They’re subtracted from the proposed design. The annual energy cost is calculated from the energy and the proposed design’s rate until you type your own. | New Off-Site Renewable Energy Production: electricity from new off-site renewable systems contracted for the project, as Tier 2 new off-site or community renewable energy. Select + Add and enter the source, the procurement, the energy and its grid region. With Same as the project, InverseHub uses the grid region in the project’s General Information. These rows count only toward the GHG emissions of LEED v4 with the 2024 energy update, so they aren’t in SimReader’s totals. See LEED and other programs. | Energy Summary by End Use: energy, demand and savings by end use. Tick Process for end uses that are process loads. | Total Energy Performance and Simulation Information: totals, process load share and unmet load hours. A total over 300 unmet hours is shown in red. | .

118.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
118.title: Upload to InverseHub
118.content: . | Select Upload to InverseHub. You need to be signed in (Settings > Sign in). | If the phase doesn’t exist on InverseHub yet, SimReader asks whether to create it. If it already has results, SimReader asks before replacing them. | Refresh the project page in InverseHub to see the new results. | . The upload also fills Simulation Program and Weather File in the project’s Energy Model Information.

119.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
119.title: Save your SimReader project
119.content: Use Save or Save As (Ctrl+S, Ctrl+Shift+S) to keep the file lists, the entries you added and the results in a .ine file. Open (Ctrl+O) brings them back later.

120.doc: Read and upload results with SimReader
120.title: After the upload: split an end use
120.content: Simulation programs have a fixed set of end uses. To report part of one separately, for example the parking garage fans inside miscellaneous equipment: . | In InverseHub, on Energy Summary by End Use, select Split an end use (+). | Choose the end use to split, tick Process load if the new end use is one, and enter its consumption and demand. | Select the new end use’s name later to edit or delete it. | . Splitting isn’t available for Parametric Analysis projects. Next: Fill in Energy Model Inputs .

122.title: Troubleshooting
122.content: Find the message you see, then what to do about it. On this page . | SimReader: reading files | SimReader: signing in and uploading | InverseHub | .

123.title: SimReader: reading files
123.content: | Message | What to do | . | Report tables missing: this EnergyPlus report is missing tables SimReader needs | Add the output tables to the IDF and rerun the simulation. See EnergyPlus and OpenStudio. | . | ES-D report missing: the .sim file has no ES-D report | The eQUEST model has no utility rates. Add them and rerun the simulation. | . | Meter name warning: meters with the same first 4 characters | eQUEST’s ES-D report keeps only 4 characters of a meter name. Rename one meter in the model so the first 4 characters differ. | . | Utility rate warning after reading | The baseline and proposed models use different rate names for a meter, so the designs are priced differently. Check the rates in both models. | . | File not found | The file was moved or renamed. Update the file list on the Project page. | . | Read error or Report files can’t be read | Check that the simulation finished and the file is complete, then select Reload. | . | Same file as baseline and proposed | The savings would be zero. Add the proposed design’s own file. To report one design only, use a Parametric Analysis project and choose Parametric Analysis in SimReader. | . | More than one proposed file | The proposed results are averaged. Keep one file unless you mean to average. | . | More than one base design file | Parametric Analysis uses only the first base design file. | . | Files missing: add the base design file | A Parametric Analysis needs a base design file before it can read the ECMs. | . | Open failed | The .ine file isn’t a SimReader project or is damaged. | .

124.title: SimReader: signing in and uploading
124.content: | Message | What to do | . | Sign in required | Go to Settings > Sign in. | . | The email or password is incorrect | Check both. If you just signed up, confirm your email first. | . | No pinned projects | Pin the project in InverseHub, then select Refresh in SimReader. See Pin the projects you’re working on. | . | No project selected | Choose the project on the Project page, then upload again. | . | Create a modeling phase? | The phase doesn’t exist on InverseHub yet. Select Create and upload. | . | Replace results on InverseHub? | The phase already has results. Select Replace to replace them. | . | Change the client? | The client you chose differs from InverseHub’s. The change applies to every phase of the project. | . | Analysis type set from InverseHub | The project’s type differs from the one SimReader had selected, so SimReader switched. Check that your files are in the right lists. | . | The project’s analysis type in InverseHub isn’t the one selected in SimReader | The project’s type was changed after you chose it. Select Reload from InverseHub, check the file lists, then upload again. | . | Upload failed | Sign out and sign in again under Settings, then try again. If it still fails, email support@inversenergy.com. | . | Upload stopped: more than one phase with this name | Email support@inversenergy.com with the project name. | . | The maximum number of projects | Your plan’s monthly project limit is reached. See Subscription plans. | .

125.title: InverseHub
125.content: | What you see | What to do | . | New results don’t appear after an upload | Refresh the page, and check the Modeling Phase selected at the top. | . | A path you need isn’t in the Rating System list | Each code lists only its own compliance paths. Check the Energy Code Used. For an IECC project that uses ASHRAE 90.1 instead, choose the 90.1 edition as the code. | . | “Select a BPF … under Performance Calculations first” | Add the performance calculation (+) before the conclusion. | . | “Enter the required energy credits … first” | Add the cost budget calculation (+) with the credits, then the conclusion. | . | “Select the eGRID subregion under zEPI Calculations first” | Add the zEPI calculation (+) with the subregion, then the conclusion. | . | “Pick the project’s province or territory under General Information” | A LEED project in Canada needs its province or territory for its GHG factors. Choose it in eGRID Subregion under General Information, then add the conclusion. | . | “That code isn’t right, or it has expired” when commenting | Use the most recent code email, within 15 minutes, or select Send a New Code. After five wrong tries, send a new code. | . | “Too many codes were sent to this email” | Five codes an hour can go to one email. Wait an hour, or use your invitation’s link. | . | “Only the client and the people the modeler invited can comment” | The modeler limited comments to the client and the project team. Use the email your invitation came to, or ask the modeler to invite you. | . | View only on a report, or “Only the client can comment” | Only the project’s client can comment on this report. You can still read it and download the PDF. | . | “InverseHub has no tables for this code and climate zone yet” in Fill Baseline | Fill those Baseline rows yourself. See What gets filled. | . | Values like “x.xx EER” after Fill Baseline | They’re placeholders. Replace them with your project’s values. | . | A red note that the code doesn’t allow the method | You picked a calculation method the code doesn’t use. The result is for reference only. Pick the code’s method in the calculation dialog. | . | Monthly Project Limit Reached | Wait for next month’s reset, or upgrade your plan. See Subscription plans. | . Still stuck? Email support@inversenergy.com with the project name, the phase and a screenshot of the message.
